title: Nonmonotone Argument and Radial Angle of a Support Slit
author: Alec Kriebel
status: Unrefereed AI-assisted preprint; conditional editorial candidate held pending independent mathematical review
original_abstract: We give negative answers to the two slit-monotonicity questions of P. L. Duren recorded as Problem 6.72 in Hayman–Lingham. Every global maximizer of the real part of a₂+i10⁻²⁴(a₄−3a₃) in the normalized schlicht class omits an arc with nonmonotone continuous argument and nonmonotone radial angle, under both signed and ordinary unsigned conventions. The proof uses classical support-point geometry, a quantitative area-theorem estimate for the actual slit tip, and controlled inversion of the Schiffer differential. It establishes actual extremizers by compactness and does not assume that an arbitrary trajectory is an extremal slit. No formula for the maximizing function or uniqueness is required. This is an unrefereed AI-assisted research note.

accessible_explanation: This unrefereed AI-assisted note studies two questions attributed to P. L. Duren about the arc omitted by a normalized univalent support point: must its polar argument and its radial angle be monotone? It claims that every global maximizer of Re[a₂+i10⁻²⁴(a₄−3a₃)] violates both properties, including the ordinary unsigned radial-angle convention. The proposed proof combines classical support-slit geometry with quantitative control of the actual slit tip and a Schiffer natural coordinate. It requires no explicit maximizing function or uniqueness. The classical methods are credited, and historical priority is not fully cleared.
central_result: Author claim: global maximizers of Re[a2+i epsilon(a4-3a3)] in S exist for epsilon=10^-24, and every such maximizer has an omitted analytic slit whose continuous polar argument, signed outward radial angle and ordinary unsigned outward radial angle are all nonmonotone.
